passages.t: ‘Oh, that I had wings like a dove!’
passages.happening:
The psalm begins with a man at the end of his strength. “Listen to my prayer, O God, and do not ignore my plea” (verse 1). He is “restless” and “distraught” (verse 2). “My heart murmurs within me, and the terrors of death assail me. Fear and trembling grip me, and horror has overwhelmed me” (verses 4 and 5).

He wishes he could escape. “I said, ‘Oh, that I had wings like a dove! I would fly away and find rest’” (verse 6). He would go far into the wilderness, “far from this raging tempest” (verse 8).

Then he looks at his city. “I see violence and strife in the city” (verse 9). People patrol its walls day and night, but the danger is inside. “Destruction is within; oppression and deceit never leave the streets” (verse 11).
passages.hearers:
The heading names no event. Many readers, old and new, have linked the psalm with Absalom's revolt against his father David (2 Samuel 15 to 17). Jerusalem was full of plotting then, and David's own trusted adviser, Ahithophel, joined the rebels. “Ahithophel is among the conspirators with Absalom” (2 Samuel 15:31). The fit is close, but the psalm does not name him. Others think it was written for anyone, in any age, betrayed in a city gone bad.

The dove was a common bird in Israel. It nests in cliffs and wild places, far from people. Doves are also gentle and easily frightened. The wish to fly away is a frightened person's wish.

City walls were meant to keep danger out. Here the walls are fine, and the city is rotten within.
passages.later:
Elijah, at the end of his strength, went into the wilderness and sat down under a tree (1 Kings 19:4). God did not scold him. He let him sleep and gave him food.

Jesus wept over Jerusalem too: “how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, but you were unwilling!” (Matthew 23:37).
passages.asks:
The wish to run away is honest, and the psalm does not hide it. Sometimes stepping away is wise. But this psalmist does not stay in the wish. He tells God about it, and then he keeps praying.

If you feel ‘fear and trembling’ like this, you are not alone and you are not weak. Tell God, and tell someone you trust.

passages.t: ‘It is you, my companion’, and ‘Cast your burden upon the LORD’
passages.happening:
Now the deepest wound comes out. “For it is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure” (verse 12). “But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend. We shared sweet fellowship together; we walked with the crowd into the house of God” (verses 13 and 14).

He prays hard words against those who did it (verse 15). Then he turns. “But I call to God, and the LORD saves me. Morning, noon, and night, I cry out in distress, and He hears my voice” (verses 16 and 17).

He looks at the friend once more. “His speech is smooth as butter, but war is in his heart. His words are softer than oil, yet they are swords unsheathed” (verse 21).

Then a word to anyone listening. “Cast your burden upon the LORD and He will sustain you; He will never let the righteous be shaken” (verse 22). The last words are short: “But I will trust in You” (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
In the ancient world, sharing a meal or going to worship together made a bond of loyalty. Friendship was not casual. That is why the friend “violates his covenant” (verse 20), his sworn bond. To betray a friend you had prayed beside was a deep wrong.

Praying ‘morning, noon, and night’ was a pattern of faithful prayer. Daniel later prayed “three times a day” toward Jerusalem (Daniel 6:10).

‘Go down to Sheol alive’ (verse 15) recalls the rebels in the wilderness, when “the earth opens its mouth and swallows them” (Numbers 16:30).
passages.later:
Jesus was betrayed by a friend he had eaten with. “Judas, are you betraying the Son of Man with a kiss?” (Luke 22:48). He knew this psalm's pain from the inside.

Peter takes up verse 22 and makes it gentle: “Cast all your anxiety on Him, because He cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7).
passages.hard: How can the psalmist pray that his enemies go down to Sheol alive (verse 15)? This is one of the prayers for judgment the book page calls the cursing psalms. It explains the main ways Christians read them. Here it is enough to say that he hands the matter to God and does not take revenge himself.
passages.asks:
If you have been betrayed by someone close, this psalm knows. It says that a friend's betrayal hurts more than an enemy's attack, and that is true. Your pain is not an overreaction. Be slow to trust smooth words again, and be gentle with yourself. If the betrayal has left you in danger, or you are afraid of someone, please tell someone you trust. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

‘Cast your burden’ does not mean the burden is small. It means it is too heavy for you and not too heavy for God. Throw it on him, again and again, morning, noon and night.
